title: Negotiation of Meaning — Interaction That Teaches

pts: Negotiation of meaning — clarification requests, confirmation checks, comprehension checks — is argued to make input more comprehensible in the moment it's needed most.
This repair process is theorised to connect input, output and attention in a way that drives acquisition.
This directly extends Tier I's Interaction Hypothesis preview (Unit 3) into a full mechanism.

v: A transcript of a pair task (recorded or provided)

items: Record two learners doing an information-gap task, or use the transcript in the model language.
Find every moment where one speaker signals a problem.
Label the moves: clarification request (CR), confirmation check (CC), comprehension check (CompC).
Mark the trigger and what the speaker did in response.
In a DIET session, groups compare transcripts from different classes.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A transcript (written for this book), with the sequence labelled:

lines: A: Put the pot on the shelf. (trigger)
B: Which shelf? (CR, indicator)
A: The top one, near the window. (response)
B: Top shelf near the window. OK. (reaction)
A: You understand? (CompC)
B: So the small pot, not the big one? (CC)

blocks.x: These are the three moves Long (1983) described, argued to make input comprehensible when it is needed most.

pts: A clarification request ('sorry, what do you mean?') pushes the speaker to reformulate, often producing more comprehensible input.
Teach these phrases explicitly as usable classroom language, not just hope learners produce them spontaneously.
This connects to Unit 27's strategic competence as a taught, not incidental, skill.

v: Chart paper; a short listening text

items: Read a short text aloud quickly, with one or two unusual words.
Ask: what could you say when you don’t understand? Collect ideas, in any language.
Build a wall chart of English repair phrases, from simple to more polite.
Read the text again; learners must use at least one phrase to stop you.
Keep the chart on the wall and point to it during every pair task.
Give each learner a ‘repair card’ with one phrase; they must use it once during the lesson.
Support: phrases with home-language equivalents.
Challenge: add phrases that ask about one specific word (What does… mean?).

lines: Sorry? / Again, please. / Can you say that again, please? / What do you mean? / Sorry, what does ‘…’ mean? / Could you explain that in a different way?
T: The farmer used a harrow on the field.
S1: Sorry, what does ‘harrow’ mean?
T: Good question. It’s a tool with spikes that breaks up the soil after ploughing.

blocks.x: A clarification request pushes the speaker to reformulate, often producing more comprehensible input. Teach these phrases explicitly; they are part of the strategic competence described in Unit 27.

body: Purpose: to show a classroom repair chart. Content: a wall chart titled ‘When you don’t understand’ with six phrases in speech bubbles, simplest at the bottom; a learner points to it. Style: bright, classroom poster. Board version: a column of phrases.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable repair wall.

body: Many learners believe that asking the teacher to repeat something is rude. Say clearly, and more than once, that asking is polite and helpful in English lessons, and thank learners every time they do it.

pts: A confirmation check ('so you mean...?') lets a listener verify understanding before the conversation moves on.
This reduces the accumulation of small misunderstandings that can derail a longer task.
Model this explicitly in task instructions before asking learners to use it independently.

v: Simple picture instructions for a rangoli design

items: Model a confirmation check: describe a simple shape and ask a learner to repeat back what they understood.
Learner A has a completed rangoli design; Learner B has a blank grid.
A describes the design step by step; B must confirm each step before drawing.
Compare drawings with the original.
Use a floor plan or a simple science diagram.
Support: a grid with numbered squares.
Challenge: B may not see A’s gestures (seated back to back).

lines: So you mean…? / You said…, right? / Is that… or…?
A: Draw a small circle in the middle.
B: So, the circle is in the centre square, right?
A: Yes. Then four petals round it.
B: Four petals, one on each side?
A: Yes, like a flower.

blocks.x: A confirmation check lets a listener verify understanding before the conversation moves on. It stops small misunderstandings building up. Model it before learners use it independently.

body: Purpose: to show confirmation in action. Content: two learners back to back; one holds a finished rangoli design, the other has a pencil above a grid and a speech bubble So you mean…? Style: warm, detailed rangoli pattern. Board version: a grid and a simple flower.

items: Excalidraw (free) for a shared drawing grid if devices are available.

points.sub: The gap has to be real
pts: Genuine information-gap and opinion-gap tasks generate far more negotiation than tasks with no real gap to bridge.
A task where one learner already knows what the other will say produces little authentic repair work.
This connects directly to Unit 3's information-gap principle and Unit 28's task design criteria.

v: Two diary pages with different appointments

items: Learner A and Learner B each receive a diary for the same week, with different appointments.
They must find a time to meet for two hours to prepare a science project.
They may not show each other their diaries.
Pairs report the time they chose and how they found it.
Three-way version: add Learner C, with a third diary.
Support: fewer appointments and a list of days on the board.
Challenge: add a rule (No meetings after 6 p.m. on school days).

lines: A: Monday 4–6 cricket practice. Wednesday 5–7 tuition. Saturday 10–12 temple with family.
B: Tuesday 4–5 dance class. Wednesday 3–5 dentist. Saturday 11–1 cousin’s birthday.
A: Are you free on Wednesday evening?
B: Wednesday… until five I’m at the dentist.
A: Until five? Then after five?
B: Yes, but you have tuition, no?

blocks.x: Tasks in which information must be exchanged by both learners (two-way), and which lead to one agreed outcome, tend to produce more negotiation than one-way or open-ended tasks (Pica, Kanagy and Falodun 1993). A task where one learner already knows what the other will say produces little repair. This builds on the information-gap principle of Unit 3 and the task criteria of Unit 28.

body: Purpose: to show a two-way information gap. Content: two diary pages side by side with coloured blocks for appointments; between them, a single highlighted slot where both are free, with a question mark leading to a tick. Style: planner-like. Board version: two weekly grids.

items: Google Docs (free) for preparing A and B versions.

blocks.x: Two photocopied or hand-copied diary pages.

pts: After a negotiation sequence, learners often reformulate their own output — modified output — moving closer to target forms.
This self-correction under communicative pressure is argued to be more durable than externally supplied correction alone.
Design tasks that give a second chance to express the same idea, prompting this reformulation naturally.
points.who: Merrill Swain's Output Hypothesis, applied to negotiation

v: Pictures of unusual objects or scenes

items: Learner A describes a picture to B, who cannot see it.
B asks at least two clarification or confirmation questions.
A reformulates in response.
A then describes the same picture to a new partner, C, without help.
A writes a one-paragraph description after the second telling.
Support: a word bank for positions and shapes.
Challenge: describe an abstract painting or a diagram from science.

blocks.x: A first attempt and its repair:

lines: A: There is a man, he is sell… selling small… small thing for hair.
B: For hair? You mean a comb?
A: No, like flowers for hair. Jasmine. He is selling jasmine strings.
There is a man selling jasmine strings for women’s hair, near the temple gate.

blocks.x: Pushed by a listener’s signal, learners often reformulate their own output, moving closer to target forms. Swain (1995) argues that producing output in this way helps learners notice gaps in their language. Giving a second chance to express the same idea prompts reformulation naturally.

body: Purpose: to show modified output. Content: two speech bubbles from the same learner: a first, broken bubble with gaps, and a second, smoother bubble; between them a small bubble from a partner, You mean…? Style: clear, sequential. Board version: two bubbles and an arrow.

pts: Teachers can model negotiation of meaning explicitly by genuinely checking their own understanding of learner output.
This shows negotiation as a normal, unremarkable part of communication, not a sign of language failure.
Avoid the reflex of simply supplying the correct form immediately — model the negotiation process instead, sometimes.

v: A phone recorder; a tally sheet

items: Record ten minutes of your own interaction with learners.
Find moments where a learner’s meaning was unclear.
Tally what you did: supplied the correct form, recast it, or asked a genuine clarification question.
In the next lesson, try to respond to at least five unclear moments with a real question first.
Compare how much learners said in response.
A colleague tallies your moves instead (Unit 68).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Two responses to the same learner turn:

lines: S1: Yesterday my uncle… he came with the thing for climbing coconut tree.

blocks.x: T (supplying): A ladder. Good. T (negotiating): For climbing? Tell me more. What does it look like?

lines: S1: It is rope, round, you put on your feet.
T: Ah, a climbing loop. Interesting. Did he climb the tree?

blocks.x: The second response treats the learner as someone with something to say. It shows negotiation as a normal part of communication, not a sign of failure. Prompts that ask learners to reformulate for themselves, rather than being given the answer, have been associated with more learner repair (Lyster and Ranta 1997). The point is balance: supply the form sometimes, negotiate at other times.

body: Purpose: to compare supplying and negotiating. Content: two panels; in one the teacher hands over a card labelled ladder and the learner falls silent; in the other the teacher asks and the learner explains with gestures. Style: gentle, observational. Board version: not applicable.

items: Audacity (free) for finding and clipping moments in a lesson recording.

blocks.x: A colleague with a tally sheet at the back of the room.

points.sub: A design problem, not a learner one
pts: If a task produces little negotiation, the likely cause is the task design, not the learners' unwillingness to communicate.
Check for a genuine gap, appropriate difficulty, and sufficient interactional demand before concluding otherwise.
This connects to Unit 22's willingness-to-communicate model — the context often explains the absence more than the learner does.

v: One task that produced little talk

items: Choose a task that produced little negotiation.
Check it against the diagnostic questions (see model language).
Identify the most likely cause.
Redesign the task to remove it.
Try the redesigned task and compare.
Colleagues redesign each other’s ‘quiet tasks’.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Is there a real gap that both partners must bridge?
Is the task too easy (no need to ask) or too hard (nothing to say)?
Can learners complete it by pointing or copying?
Do learners feel safe enough to ask (Unit 22)?
Before: Read the text and answer questions with your partner. (Both have the text; nothing to negotiate.)
After: A has paragraphs 1–2, B has 3–4. Answer the questions together without showing your text.

blocks.x: If a task produces little negotiation, the likely cause is the task design, not unwilling learners. As the willingness-to-communicate model in Unit 22 suggests, context often explains the silence more than the learner does.

body: Purpose: to show task diagnosis. Content: a pair of learners sitting silently with the same sheet; a magnifying glass reveals the cause, ‘No gap’; beside it, a redesigned pair with split sheets, talking. Style: problem-and-solution. Board version: two pairs of stick figures.

points.sub: Not every gap needs closing live
pts: Excessive negotiation can also fragment a task's communicative flow if overused or poorly timed.
Some negotiation is best noted and addressed in the post-task language focus stage instead of resolved mid-task.
This is a judgement call, connecting back to Unit 8's guidance on when to correct immediately versus delay.

items: Label a corner of the board ‘Parking’.
During a task, if a pair cannot resolve a word or form quickly, they write it on a slip and park it.
Pairs continue the task using whatever strategy works (a gesture, a home-language word, a description).
In the language focus stage, go through the parked items with the class.
Use a shared online board so that parked items are saved for the next lesson.
Support: the teacher parks items for a pair that is struggling.
Challenge: learners try to answer parked items for other pairs before the teacher does.

lines: How to say ‘chakli’? → a spiral, crunchy snack made from rice flour
I am knowing him since five years. → I have known him for five years

blocks.x: Too much negotiation can fragment a task’s flow. Some problems are best noted and dealt with after the task, in the language focus stage (Unit 28). Deciding which to resolve now and which to park is a judgement call, like the choice between immediate and delayed correction in Unit 8.

body: Purpose: to show deferred negotiation. Content: a board corner with a ‘P’ sign and slips under it; pairs keep talking while one learner carries a slip to the board. Style: light, practical. Board version: a box with a P and slips.

body: For one week, respond to every unclear learner answer with a genuine question before giving any correction. Count how many learners reformulate on their own. Then add a parking board to your next task and compare the flow.

dek: Unit 30 of 100: when communication breaks down and gets repaired in real time, that repair work is argued to be where much of second language acquisition actually happens.

aims.x: This unit examines negotiation of meaning: the moments when communication breaks down and speakers work together to repair it. The Interaction Hypothesis argues that this repair work is one of the places where acquisition happens. The unit shows how to teach the language of repair, how to design tasks that generate it, how teachers can model it, and when it is better left until after a task.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain the Interaction Hypothesis and the role of negotiation in it;
identify clarification requests, confirmation checks and comprehension checks in real talk;
teach repair phrases as usable classroom language;
design two-way information-gap tasks that require negotiation;
create opportunities for modified output;
model negotiation in your own teacher talk;
diagnose why a task is producing little negotiation;

why: Why this matters. Smooth communication feels like the goal, but a certain amount of productive breakdown-and-repair may be doing more acquisition work than smoothness ever could.

background.x: In the early 1980s Michael Long studied conversations between native and non-native speakers and noticed that what changed most was not the grammar of the input but the structure of the interaction. Speakers checked, clarified, repeated and rephrased (Long 1983). He argued that these interactional modifications make input comprehensible exactly when the learner needs it. Long (1996) later proposed that negotiation connects input, internal learner capacities (especially selective attention) and output in productive ways. Evelyn Varonis and Susan Gass (1985) described the typical shape of a negotiation sequence: a trigger, an indicator of difficulty, a response and a reaction.

Merrill Swain (1985, 1995) added a complementary point from her research in Canadian immersion programmes: learners who receive a great deal of input may still not develop accurate production unless they are pushed to produce output. When a listener signals difficulty, the speaker must reformulate, and this modified output may help them notice gaps in their own language. Teresa Pica (1994) concluded that negotiation aids comprehension and draws attention to form, while cautioning about how much it can do alone, and Pauline Foster (1998) found far less negotiation in real classrooms than laboratory studies suggested. The lesson for teachers is that negotiation does not happen automatically; it must be designed for.

In many Indian classrooms, interaction follows the pattern of teacher question, learner answer and teacher evaluation. Many learners feel it would be impolite to ask the teacher what something means. Yet the same learners negotiate meaning skilfully every day, moving between Kannada, Urdu, Tamil, Hindi and English with friends and neighbours. The NEP 2020 recognizes this multilingual competence as a resource (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). The task for the English teacher is to make repair a normal, polite and expected part of English lessons, and to design tasks in which it is necessary.

items: Repair phrase use. Tally the repair phrases each pair uses during an information-gap task.
Modified output. Compare first and second tellings of the same description for clarity and accuracy.
Task outcome. Check whether two-way tasks were completed accurately (diaries matched, drawings correct).
Teacher talk audit. Repeat the negotiate-or-supply tally once a term.
Do your learners ever ask you to repeat or explain? If not, why not?
Which of your tasks have a genuine two-way gap?
What do you usually do when a learner’s meaning is unclear?
How do your learners negotiate meaning in their home languages, and can that help in English?
When do you let a misunderstanding pass for the sake of flow?
What would change if asking questions earned praise in your class?

terms.def: A move asking a speaker to repeat or explain what they said, such as ‘Sorry, what do you mean?’; it serves both negotiation of meaning and implicit error correction.
A question asked to see whether a listener has understood, such as ‘Is that clear?’ or ‘Do you follow?’; used in negotiation of meaning.
A question that checks whether one has understood a speaker correctly, often by repeating their words, such as ‘You mean Tuesday?’
An activity in which learners hold different information and must communicate to complete a task, such as finding differences between two pictures or completing a timetable.
The proposal that conversational interaction, especially negotiation of meaning, promotes acquisition by making input comprehensible and drawing attention to form (Long 1996).
A change speakers make to conversation to overcome communication problems, such as a clarification request, confirmation check or repetition. It is central to negotiation of meaning.
Output that a learner reformulates after a signal of difficulty from a listener, such as a clarification request; the effort may help the learner notice gaps in their own language.
The interactional work, such as clarification requests and comprehension checks, that speakers do to resolve breakdowns in understanding; it is claimed to help acquisition (Long 1996).
Output that learners are pushed to make more accurate, precise or appropriate, for example by a request to reformulate; producing it may help them notice gaps and promote acquisition (Swain 1985).
A task in which each participant holds information the other needs, so that both must exchange information to complete it. It generates more negotiation of meaning than a one-way task.
